title: Google ships Gemini 3.8 Live for production voice agents
subtitle: A cost-optimized live model and an Extended Thinking variant that speaks while reasoning ship across the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and Workspace.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google announced Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking on September 15, 2026, rolling both out across the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Gemini Enterprise, Search Live, Gemini Live, and Google Workspace. The pair splits the workload: Gemini 3.8 Live is positioned as the fast, cost-efficient conversational model, and Extended Thinking is built for high-complexity tasks that need multi-step reasoning — and, notably, can speak while it is reasoning and while it is running tools. Google reports Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking at 82.6 on Artificial Analysis' Speech-to-Speech Quality Index, 68.6% on τ-Voice for agentic task completion, 35.1% on Sierra's τ-Voice-banking, and 97.7% on Big Bench Audio.

The capability change worth naming is "speak while reasoning." Prior generations of voice models finished thinking, then spoke; users heard silence during multi-step tool calls, which broke the conversational illusion and made voice agents feel more brittle than their text counterparts. A model that can narrate its reasoning aloud — "let me pull that up for you" — while it is still actually executing the check, is a materially different UX. It is also new safety surface: what the model says out loud during a tool call becomes something to test for hallucination, deception, and leakage of intermediate state.

Google shipped this at less than half the per-token price of OpenAI's GPT-Live-1, according to the coverage — continuing a 2026 pattern of Google pricing aggressively on voice and Enterprise workloads specifically. The strategic bet is that voice becomes the default agent interface for customer service, appointment setting, and in-workspace copilots, and that owning the whole low-latency stack (model, TTS, ASR, tool orchestration) matters more than owning the raw benchmark top spot on any single dimension.

Takeaway for learners: voice AI is a great early-career specialty right now. The field is small, the failure modes are visible in real time, and the evaluation methods are still being invented. If you can run a τ-Voice-style benchmark, explain what barge-in is and why it is hard, and reason about a sub-300ms latency budget end-to-end, you are already ahead of most application developers building on top of these models — and there is a growing catalog of jobs in that gap.
